items.followUp: Define respiration and write its balanced equation.

rubric.why: A definition must state that plants use light energy to make food.
rubric.description: Defines photosynthesis as the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential idea that green plants use light energy to make food; the raw materials may also be mentioned. Oxygen may be identified as a product rather than part of the definition.

rubric.why: The balanced equation gives the reactants and products of photosynthesis in the correct proportions.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation, including carbon dioxide and water as reactants and glucose and oxygen as products.

modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy, in the presence of chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O —(light, chlorophyll)→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

items.followUp: What is the dark reaction of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: The light reaction depends on light captured by chlorophyll and converts it into chemical energy.
rubric.description: States that the reaction occurs in light and that chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is converted into chemical energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking light and chlorophyll with the conversion of light energy to chemical energy.

rubric.why: Splitting water supplies products used in photosynthesis and releases oxygen.
rubric.description: Mentions splitting of water and release of oxygen, or the formation of ATP and NADPH in the light reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the water-splitting and oxygen-release point or the formation of ATP and NADPH.

modelAnswer: The light reaction is the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis in which chlorophyll absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy stored in ATP and NADPH.
Water is split (photolysis), releasing oxygen.

items.followUp: Give one example each of an intracellular and an extracellular enzyme.

rubric.why: The key distinction is where the enzyme performs its action.
rubric.description: States that intracellular enzymes act inside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the site of action as inside the cell.

rubric.why: Extracellular enzymes are released to act outside the cells that produce them.
rubric.description: States that extracellular enzymes are secreted and act outside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying secretion or action outside the cell.

modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes are produced and act inside the cells in which they are made.
Extracellular enzymes are produced by cells and secreted to act outside those cells.

items.followUp: Describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.

rubric.why: The induced-fit model is the suitable model because it accounts for the active site changing shape when the substrate binds.
rubric.description: Names the induced-fit model and states that the enzyme's active site is flexible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the induced-fit model or clearly describing a flexible active site.

rubric.why: Binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex and brings about a fit between enzyme and substrate.
rubric.description: Explains that substrate binding changes the active-site shape to fit the substrate and form an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the binding-and-fit explanation; accept equivalent wording.

modelAnswer: The induced-fit model is the suitable model of enzyme action.
The enzyme's active site is flexible; when a substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.

items.followUp: Draw and label the small intestine.

rubric.why: A recognizable stomach outline with its main regions is needed for a labeled biological diagram.
rubric.description: Draws a recognizable, curved, sac-like stomach outline, including its upper fundus and main body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognizable stomach shape with the fundus and body indicated.

rubric.why: The entry and exit connections identify the stomach and its orientation.
rubric.description: Labels the oesophagus entry and the pyloric outlet leading to the duodenum; accept the cardiac sphincter as an entry label.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct entry and outlet labels, including the duodenum.

modelAnswer: Draw a curved, J-shaped sac with a rounded upper part (fundus), a central body and a narrower lower end.
Draw the oesophagus entering at the upper end and the duodenum leaving the lower end.
Label the fundus, body, oesophagus, pyloric sphincter and duodenum.

items.followUp: Name the two vascular tissues in plants and state what each transports.

rubric.why: The plant vascular system is made up of the conducting tissues xylem and phloem.
rubric.description: Identifies xylem and phloem as the plant vascular tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both xylem and phloem.

rubric.why: The vascular system transports materials throughout the plant.
rubric.description: Defines the vascular system as the conducting system that transports materials through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it conducts or transports substances through the plant.

modelAnswer: The vascular system is the system of conducting tissues that transports materials throughout a plant.
It consists of xylem and phloem.

items.followUp: List four occupations related to the study of biology.

rubric.why: Medicine is a profession that can be pursued after biological studies.
rubric.description: Names one biology-related profession in medicine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid medical profession, such as doctor, physician or surgeon.

rubric.why: Pharmacy is a profession that uses biological knowledge.
rubric.description: Names pharmacy or a pharmacist as a profession.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pharmacist or pharmacy.

rubric.why: Agriculture-related careers apply biological knowledge to crops and farming.
rubric.description: Names one profession related to agriculture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid agriculture-related profession.

rubric.why: Biology also leads to careers in research, biotechnology and teaching.
rubric.description: Names one other valid biology-related profession.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid profession, such as biologist, biotechnologist, researcher or biology teacher. Award no more than 4 marks overall.

modelAnswer: Doctor or physician.
Pharmacist.
Agriculturist.
Biologist or biological researcher.

items.followUp: Explain how water and minerals are transported from the roots to the leaves of a plant.

rubric.why: Food is transported through the phloem, not the xylem.
rubric.description: Identifies phloem as the tissue that transports food in plants.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem as the food-conducting tissue.

rubric.why: Food moves from places where it is made or released (sources) to places where it is used or stored (sinks).
rubric.description: Explains that food moves from a source, such as a leaf, to a sink, such as a growing or storage organ.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing movement from source to sink.

rubric.why: Loading food into the sieve tubes is part of the translocation process.
rubric.description: States that sucrose is loaded into the phloem sieve tubes, with the help of companion cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for sucrose loading into sieve tubes or an equivalent correct description of phloem loading.

rubric.why: Water entering the phloem raises pressure and helps drive the movement of food sap.
rubric.description: Explains that water enters the phloem by osmosis, creating pressure that moves the food sap.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the osmosis-and-pressure explanation.

rubric.why: A pressure difference drives phloem sap toward sinks, where food is removed for use or storage.
rubric.description: States that sap moves from higher pressure at the source toward lower pressure at the sink, where food is unloaded.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pressure-driven movement toward the sink and/or food unloading there.

modelAnswer: Food made in leaves is transported to other parts of the plant through the phloem; this movement is called translocation.
At a source, sucrose is loaded into the phloem sieve tubes, with the help of companion cells.
Water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis, increasing pressure in the phloem sap.
The pressure difference drives the sap from the source, where pressure is high, toward sinks, where pressure is lower.
At sinks, food is unloaded and used or stored; water can return to the xylem.
